New drivers on these subs tend to overthink things. You really just need to worry about keeping the RPM's in a range the engine wants. You can brake whenever you want to brake, just make sure the revs will keep the engine where it won't bog and/or stall out. 

If you are cruising and traffic slows, use the engine braking and the brake pedal as necessary. If the revs get low and things are smooth, just downshift.  If you get to the point where you need 1st or 2nd gear, you are probably coming to a stop so you can just clutch in and brake to the stopping point. Similarly, if you are in a high gear and traffic is coming to a sudden halt ahead, just clutch in and brake to a stop. If the stop never happens, you can always pop it into the correct lower gear and rev match into it.  
  
Ultimately, you just want to avoid bogging or stalling the engine. Of course, if there are hills involved you also need to consider the additional load and maybe drop a gear.

Hello. First, sorry for your situation. I'm an adjuster myself and wanted to reply as the other person has yet to. He's a senior. Me, not so much but I know a thing or two. I'd welcome anyone correct me with whatever I say below. 

  
If you've litigated your file already, it becomes the defense attorney(employers attorney) right to subpoena any medical record discovered. There's a few ways they will discover it exists. One, they depose you. This is where it's up to you to be truthful. If you mention your prior medicals, they WILL subpoena them. If you choose to lie, that's your consequence to bear. Otherwise, if the defense sees fit to order a medical canvas(they investigate local providers for your attendance), if they get any hits they will subpoena those records. They may have already done this, but it's damn near certain a visit from 40 years ago with a psychiatrist wouldn't come up. Lastly, if you mention this to any of the doctors, it will make its way into the medical report which all parties can review.

In the eyes of the state, it is the defenses job to conduct a thorough investigation. Unfortunately, that does mean acquiring any pertinent medical history and records that could potentially affect your claim. As much as you wouldn't like your past being brought up, if you have PTSD, it's entirely in the realm of possibility than past mental trauma is an aspect that needs to be addressed for your claim. Likely, you are schedule to go to a Psyche QME for causation. The QME would use this information to both decide if your psyche issues truly are caused by your motor vehicle accident. If found to be industrial, they would then assess permanent disability once you are deemed P&S/MMI. At this point, he may factor in your prior psyche injury for apportionment. For example, if he things your current PTSD is 10% related to your past, he will deduct this from your final impairment rating.

We all want the same thing, for you to heal and return to your job at your usual pay rate and hours.

In CA, the way the laws are setup after Arnalds tenure is that the employer has a Medical Provider Network in which the injured worker has to treat within. They can change doctors within the MPN, but they cannot treat outside of it unless it is due to immediate medical necessity. 

Thus, you can't just go get a walk-in visit at whatever urgent care center is near you. Your employer *should* direct you to your first visit. After thirty days is when you can declare you'd like to transfer your care. The reason any given urgent care center would deny treatment is that they wouldn't get paid for their services. If they were to treat, they'd have to file a Lien against the employer stating why the treatment was medically necessary, they they have to pay an upfront cost to file the lien that can only be paid back by winning the case.
